text: You are given a sorted array of integers and must remove the duplicates in place, returning the length of the deduplicated prefix. Describe an algorithm that does this without allocating a second array, state its time and space complexity, and say what your algorithm does when the array is empty or holds a single element.

expected_concepts.hint: one read index scanning ahead, one write index marking the deduplicated prefix
overwrites the input, returns a length; the tail beyond it is not cleaned up
O(n) time, one pass; O(1) extra space
n = 0 returns 0; n = 1 returns 1 without entering the loop

common_misconceptions: believes an in-place algorithm may still allocate an O(n) temporary buffer
returns the array rather than the length and leaves the stale tail visible
reference_answer: Keep two indices. `write` marks the end of the deduplicated prefix and starts at 1; `read` scans from index 1 to the end. Whenever a[read] differs from a[write - 1], copy it to a[write] and advance write. Because the array is sorted, all copies of a value are adjacent, so comparing against the last kept element is sufficient - no set or auxiliary array is needed. The loop touches each element once, so it is O(n) time and O(1) extra space; the O(1) claim is the point of the question, and an answer that uses a hash set has not answered it. Return write as the new length. Empty input must return 0 before the loop runs, and a single element returns 1 trivially, since write is initialised to 1 and the loop body never executes. A strong answer notes that elements beyond the returned length are left as garbage by design, which is the contract the caller must respect.
follow_up_seeds: What changes if the array is not sorted and order must be preserved?

text: A dynamic array doubles its capacity whenever it becomes full, copying every existing element into the new buffer. A colleague proposes growing by a fixed 100 elements instead, to waste less memory. Compare the total cost of appending n elements under each strategy, and explain what the phrase 'amortised O(1) append' means for the doubling version.

expected_concepts.hint: total cost over a sequence divided by the number of operations, not an average over inputs
geometric growth gives a total copy cost that is a convergent series; fixed growth does not
doubling: O(n) total, O(1) amortised. Fixed step: O(n^2/k) total, O(n) amortised
doubling wastes up to half the buffer to buy the amortised bound

common_misconceptions: treats amortised and average-case as interchangeable claims
believes doubling makes every append O(n) because some appends copy
reference_answer: Under doubling, the copies happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, ... n, so the total number of element copies is bounded by 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n < 2n. Spread over n appends, that is O(1) per append amortised, even though individual appends that trigger a resize cost O(n). Under fixed growth of k = 100, a resize happens every 100 appends and copies everything, giving 100 + 200 + ... + n = O(n^2 / k) total work - still quadratic, because dividing by a constant does not change the growth class. Amortised O(1) is a guarantee about any sequence of n operations, not a probabilistic statement: no adversarial input makes the total exceed O(n). That is what distinguishes it from average-case, which quantifies over a distribution of inputs. The cost of the guarantee is memory: immediately after a doubling, up to half the buffer is unused, which is the tradeoff the colleague is really objecting to.
follow_up_seeds: What growth factor would you pick if memory were the binding constraint?

text: In a language with immutable strings, such as Python or Java, building a result by repeatedly writing s = s + chunk inside a loop over n chunks is far slower than it looks. Explain what the runtime actually does on each iteration, give the total time complexity of the loop, and describe the idiomatic fix.

expected_concepts.hint: each concatenation allocates a new string and copies both operands
the growing prefix is recopied every iteration, giving 1 + 2 + ... + n copies
O(n * m) copies overall, quadratic in total output length
collect the pieces in a list and join once, or use a StringBuilder

common_misconceptions: assumes the compiler always rewrites the loop into a builder
believes the cost is the allocation count rather than the repeated copying
reference_answer: Because strings are immutable, s + chunk cannot extend s in place: the runtime allocates a fresh string of the combined length and copies both operands into it. The accumulated prefix therefore gets copied again on every iteration, so the total work is proportional to 1 + 2 + ... + n, that is O(n^2) in the number of chunks or, stated in characters, quadratic in the length of the final string. The fix is to stop building intermediate results: append the chunks to a list and call ''.join(parts) once in Python, or use StringBuilder in Java, both of which write into a geometrically growing buffer and produce the final string in a single pass, giving O(total length). A strong answer notes that CPython has an in-place optimisation for the special case of a string with a single reference, which is exactly why the bug survives small benchmarks and reappears in production; it is an implementation detail, not a guarantee to design around.
follow_up_seeds: Does the same reasoning apply to list concatenation in a loop?

text: Explain how a hash table resolves collisions with separate chaining, and how open addressing with linear probing differs. Give the average and the worst-case time complexity of a lookup under each, and describe an input that would push a hash table into its worst case.

expected_concepts.hint: two distinct keys landing in the same bucket must both remain findable
each bucket holds a list; lookup scans that list
probe subsequent slots in the table itself; deletion needs tombstones
O(1) average, O(n) worst case when every key collides
resize thresholds; probing degrades sharply as the table fills

common_misconceptions: states hash table lookup is O(1) with no qualification about the hash function
thinks open addressing can delete an entry by simply clearing the slot
reference_answer: With separate chaining each bucket points at a secondary structure, usually a linked list, and a lookup hashes to the bucket then scans it. With open addressing all entries live in the table itself: on a collision, linear probing inspects the next slot, and the next, until it finds the key or an empty slot. Deletion under open addressing cannot simply blank a slot, because that would truncate the probe sequence for other keys - it needs a tombstone. Both are O(1) on average given a hash function that distributes keys roughly uniformly and a bounded load factor maintained by resizing. Both are O(n) in the worst case, when every key hashes to the same bucket: chaining degenerates to scanning one long list, probing to scanning one long run. That input is reachable deliberately - an attacker who knows the hash function can craft colliding keys, which is a real denial-of-service vector and the reason production runtimes randomise their hash seeds. Linear probing additionally suffers primary clustering, so it degrades faster than chaining as the load factor approaches 1, while being friendlier to the cache at low load factors.
follow_up_seeds: Why do some standard libraries switch a bucket from a list to a tree?

text: A service stores millions of events keyed by timestamp, and its most frequent query is 'give me every event between 09:00 and 09:05'. A teammate proposes a hash map from timestamp to event because lookups are O(1). Explain why a hash map is the wrong structure for this access pattern, and what you would use instead.

expected_concepts.hint: hashing destroys order, so neighbouring keys are not neighbouring in memory
the workload is a range scan, not a point lookup
a balanced BST, skip list, B-tree or sorted array supports range scans
choose by the dominant access pattern, not by the fastest headline complexity

common_misconceptions: argues O(1) point lookup beats O(log n) regardless of the query being asked
suggests iterating the whole hash map and filtering, treating O(n) per query as acceptable
reference_answer: A hash map answers 'what is the value for exactly this key' in O(1), and nothing else. The workload described is a range scan, and a hash function deliberately destroys the ordering of keys, so there is no way to enumerate the keys between two bounds without inspecting every entry - turning each query into O(n). The correct choice is an ordered structure: a balanced binary search tree, a skip list, a B-tree, or simply a sorted array if the data is append-only in time order. All of them find the lower bound in O(log n) and then walk forward in O(k) for k matching results, which is proportional to the size of the answer rather than the size of the data. In a database this is the same argument as choosing a B-tree index over a hash index. The general principle worth stating is that a data structure is chosen by the dominant access pattern, and that O(1) for the wrong operation is worse than O(log n) for the right one.
follow_up_seeds: When would you keep both structures over the same data?

text: Given a string containing only the characters (, ), [, ], { and }, describe an algorithm that decides whether the brackets are correctly balanced and nested. Say which data structure you would use and why that structure in particular, and give the time and space complexity.

expected_concepts.hint: push openers, pop and compare on each closer
correct nesting means the most recent unmatched opener must close first
O(n) time, one pass over the string
a closer with an empty stack fails; a non-empty stack at the end also fails

common_misconceptions: counts openers and closers and concludes equal counts means balanced
forgets that leftover openers at the end of the string are a failure
reference_answer: Scan the string once. Push every opening bracket onto a stack. On every closing bracket, fail immediately if the stack is empty, otherwise pop and fail if the popped opener is not the matching type. After the scan, the string is balanced only if the stack is empty. A stack is the right structure because correct nesting is exactly a last-in-first-out constraint: the bracket that must close next is always the most recently opened unmatched one. Both failure checks matter and are the usual omission - a closing bracket with nothing to match, and unmatched openers left at the end. The algorithm is O(n) time and O(n) space in the worst case, when every character is an opening bracket. A counting approach is not equivalent: ([)] has equal counts of each type and is still incorrectly nested, which is the cleanest way to show why the order, not the tally, is what is being checked.
follow_up_seeds: How would you extend this to report the index where it first went wrong?

text: Implement a FIFO queue using only two LIFO stacks, supporting enqueue and dequeue. Describe the algorithm, then analyse the cost of a sequence of n operations. Is dequeue O(1) in the worst case, O(1) amortised, or neither?

expected_concepts.hint: FIFO built from two LIFO structures by reversing once
an inbox stack for pushes, an outbox stack that is only refilled when empty
each element is moved between stacks at most once, so n operations cost O(n)
a single dequeue can be O(n); the amortised bound is the correct claim

common_misconceptions: transfers all elements on every dequeue, making the structure genuinely O(n) per operation
claims worst-case O(1) dequeue because most dequeues are cheap
reference_answer: Keep an inbox stack and an outbox stack. Enqueue always pushes onto the inbox, which is O(1). Dequeue pops the outbox; if the outbox is empty, first pop every element from the inbox and push it onto the outbox, which reverses the order and puts the oldest element on top, then pop. The critical detail is that the transfer happens only when the outbox is empty - transferring on every dequeue destroys the bound. Each element is pushed to the inbox once, moved to the outbox at most once, and popped once, so any sequence of n operations does O(n) total work and dequeue is O(1) amortised. It is not O(1) worst case: the dequeue that triggers a transfer of k elements costs O(k). Stating the amortised bound and explicitly disclaiming the worst-case one is the answer being looked for; this is also a good example of why such a structure is unsuitable for a hard real-time deadline, where the worst case is the only number that matters.
follow_up_seeds: Where would this structure be a bad choice despite the amortised bound?

text: You need a collection that is iterated front to back constantly, with elements also inserted and removed at arbitrary positions. A colleague argues for a doubly linked list because insertion is O(1) where an array list is O(n). Explain what that argument leaves out, and what you would measure before deciding.

expected_concepts.hint: the dominant operation here is traversal, not insertion
contiguous memory prefetches well; chasing pointers does not
O(1) with a cache miss can lose to O(n) with a memcpy at realistic n
two pointers plus allocator overhead per element, and fragmented allocations

common_misconceptions: treats the asymptotic bound as the whole answer regardless of the constant factors
forgets that reaching the insertion position in a linked list is itself O(n)
reference_answer: The O(1) insertion claim is true only once you already hold a reference to the node. Reaching an arbitrary position requires walking the list, which is O(n), so for insert-at-position the two structures have the same asymptotic cost and differ only in constants. Those constants strongly favour the array: its elements are contiguous, so traversal streams through cache lines and the hardware prefetcher works, whereas each linked-list step is a dependent load into a potentially cold cache line. An array insertion is a memmove, which is one of the fastest operations a CPU performs, while a list insertion is an allocation plus pointer writes. The list also carries two pointers and allocator overhead per element, tripling memory for small payloads and worsening locality further. Given that this workload is dominated by full traversal, the array list is very likely faster, and the honest answer is to benchmark at the real n, with the real element size and the real insert-to-traversal ratio, rather than to argue from the complexity table. A list does win where insertion points are already held as references, or where stable references must survive mutation.
follow_up_seeds: At what n, and for what element size, would you expect the list to win?

text: Describe Floyd's cycle-detection algorithm for a singly linked list: how the two pointers move, why they are guaranteed to meet if a cycle exists, and how you would then locate the first node of the cycle. State its space complexity and contrast that with the hash-set approach.

expected_concepts.hint: slow moves one step, fast moves two; they meet inside the cycle or fast hits null
inside the cycle the gap closes by one per step, so it must reach zero
restart one pointer at the head and advance both by one to find the entry node
O(1) versus O(n) for a visited set

common_misconceptions: asserts the pointers meet at the start of the cycle rather than somewhere inside it
claims the fast pointer could jump over the slow one and miss it entirely
reference_answer: Advance a slow pointer one node per step and a fast pointer two. If the list terminates, fast reaches null and there is no cycle. If there is a cycle, both pointers eventually enter it, and thereafter the fast pointer gains exactly one position per step on the slow one. A gap that decreases by exactly one per step cannot be skipped over, so it must hit zero: they meet. That is the correctness argument, and it is the part most answers omit. To find the entry node, reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time; they meet at the first node of the cycle, which follows from the meeting point being congruent to the cycle entry modulo the cycle length. The algorithm uses O(1) extra space and O(n) time. The hash-set alternative - walk the list recording visited nodes and stop at the first repeat - is simpler and also O(n) time, but O(n) space, and it is the better choice when clarity matters more than memory. A strong answer names that tradeoff rather than treating Floyd's algorithm as automatically superior.
follow_up_seeds: How would you also report the length of the cycle?

text: A binary search tree is usually quoted as O(log n) for lookup. Describe an insertion sequence that reduces a plain BST to O(n) lookup, explain what a self-balancing tree such as an AVL or red-black tree does about it, and say what that balancing costs.

expected_concepts.hint: left subtree smaller, right subtree larger; lookup cost is the path length
already-sorted input produces a path, not a tree
rotations restore a height bound of O(log n) after each mutation
O(log n) is a claim about height, and height is only bounded if balance is enforced

common_misconceptions: states BST lookup is O(log n) without the balanced qualifier
believes balancing is free rather than a per-write cost
reference_answer: Lookup in a BST costs the length of the root-to-node path, so O(log n) is really a claim about the tree's height. Inserting already-sorted keys - 1, 2, 3, ... n - makes every new key the right child of the previous one, producing a linked list of height n and O(n) lookups. This is not an exotic case: inserting records in id or timestamp order is exactly what an application usually does. A self-balancing tree detects the imbalance during insertion and repairs it with rotations - AVL keeps the heights of sibling subtrees within one, red-black keeps a weaker colour invariant that bounds the height at 2 log(n + 1) - so height stays logarithmic for any insertion order. The cost is on every write: extra bookkeeping per node, up to O(log n) rotations per insertion or deletion, and more complex code. AVL is more rigidly balanced so it reads slightly faster and writes slightly slower than red-black, which is why read-heavy structures tend to choose AVL and general-purpose libraries tend to choose red-black.
follow_up_seeds: Why do databases use B-trees rather than binary balanced trees?

text: You have an unweighted graph and need the shortest path, measured in number of edges, between two nodes. Explain why breadth-first search returns the correct answer and why depth-first search does not, and state the time complexity of BFS in terms of vertices and edges.

expected_concepts.hint: a queue expands the frontier one distance level at a time
the first time BFS reaches a node is by a minimum-edge path
DFS commits to depth first, so it may reach a node by a long path before a short one
O(V + E) with an adjacency list, each vertex and edge visited once

common_misconceptions: believes DFS finds shortest paths if you keep the best distance seen
quotes O(V * E) or O(V^2) without reference to the graph representation
reference_answer: BFS expands nodes in non-decreasing order of distance from the source: it processes the whole frontier at distance d before any node at distance d + 1. Consequently the first time a node is dequeued, the path that reached it is a minimum-edge path, and marking nodes visited on enqueue keeps that property. DFS has no such ordering - it follows one branch to exhaustion, so it can reach a node by a long path first and mark it visited, never reconsidering it. DFS can be forced to produce correct distances by removing the visited-once rule and revisiting nodes when a shorter path appears, but that is no longer plain DFS and is exponential in the worst case. With an adjacency list, BFS enqueues each vertex at most once and inspects each edge at most once (twice for an undirected graph), so it is O(V + E) time and O(V) space. With an adjacency matrix it becomes O(V^2), because finding a vertex's neighbours costs a row scan - a useful reminder that complexity depends on the representation.
follow_up_seeds: How would you recover the actual path, not just its length?

text: Dijkstra's algorithm is often summarised as 'shortest path, but with weights'. Using a small concrete example, show how it can return a wrong answer when one edge has a negative weight, explain which property of the algorithm the negative edge breaks, and name an algorithm that handles negative edges correctly.

expected_concepts.hint: a settled node's distance is final, which assumes paths cannot get cheaper later
a later negative edge can undercut a distance already committed to
a concrete graph with numbers, not a verbal assertion
relaxes all edges V-1 times and can detect negative cycles

common_misconceptions: claims adding a constant to every edge weight fixes the problem
conflates negative edges with negative cycles and calls the problem undefined
reference_answer: Take S -> A with weight 2, S -> B with weight 5, and B -> A with weight -4. Dijkstra settles S, then extracts A at 2 and treats that distance as final. It later extracts B at 5 and relaxes B -> A, computing 5 + (-4) = 1 - but A is already settled, so the improvement is discarded and the algorithm reports 2 when the true shortest distance to A is 1. Note that the negative edge has to arrive after the node it improves has been settled; an example where the improvement is found while the node is still tentative will silently give the right answer and prove nothing. The property that breaks is the greedy invariant: Dijkstra assumes that once a node is extracted with the minimum tentative distance, no future relaxation can improve it, which holds only when all edge weights are non-negative, so every path extension is non-decreasing. A negative edge makes a longer path cheaper later, invalidating the finality of settled nodes. Adding a constant to all weights does not fix it, because it penalises paths in proportion to their edge count and so changes which path is shortest. Bellman-Ford is the correct algorithm: it relaxes every edge V - 1 times in O(V * E), makes no greedy commitment, and a further relaxation pass that still improves a distance proves a negative cycle exists - at which point 'shortest path' genuinely is undefined.
follow_up_seeds: When would you use Johnson's algorithm instead?

text: A build system must run tasks in an order that respects their declared dependencies, and must report a clear error when the dependencies cannot be satisfied at all. Explain how you would model this problem, which algorithm produces a valid order, and how the same algorithm detects the impossible case.

expected_concepts.hint: tasks are vertices, 'A must precede B' is a directed edge
Kahn's algorithm on in-degrees, or a DFS post-order reversed
a valid ordering exists if and only if the graph is acyclic
leftover nodes with non-zero in-degree are exactly the cycle members

common_misconceptions: assumes a topological order is unique
detects cycles with a separate traversal rather than from the sort's own residue
reference_answer: Model tasks as vertices and each 'A must run before B' as a directed edge A -> B. A valid execution order is a topological ordering, which exists exactly when the graph is a DAG. Kahn's algorithm is the practical choice: compute every in-degree, seed a queue with the zero in-degree tasks, and repeatedly emit a task and decrement its successors' in-degrees, enqueueing any that reach zero. It is O(V + E). Cycle detection falls out of the same run rather than needing a second pass: if the emitted order is shorter than the number of tasks, the tasks never emitted are precisely those still trapped by an unsatisfiable dependency, and they can be reported by name - which is what makes the error message useful. The DFS variant instead reverses the post-order and detects a cycle by finding a back edge to a node still on the recursion stack. Worth stating: the ordering is generally not unique, and the queue of zero in-degree tasks is also the set that can be executed in parallel, which is how a real build system gets its concurrency.
follow_up_seeds: How would you extend this to run independent tasks in parallel?

text: You must split an array of positive integers into exactly k contiguous parts so that the largest part sum is as small as possible. Explain how binary search applies here even though the array is not sorted: what values you search over, what property makes the search valid, and how you test one candidate value.

expected_concepts.hint: search the space of possible answers, not the array
if a limit L is achievable then every larger limit is too - the predicate is monotone
greedily fill parts up to L and count them; feasible if the count is at most k
O(n log(sum - max)) - a linear check inside a logarithmic search

common_misconceptions: believes binary search requires the input array itself to be sorted
searches over indices rather than over the answer value
reference_answer: Binary search does not need a sorted array; it needs a monotone predicate over an ordered search space. Here the search space is the candidate answer - the maximum allowed part sum L - which ranges from max(array), since no part can be smaller than its largest element, to sum(array), which is the single-part case. The predicate 'can the array be split into at most k parts each summing to at most L' is monotone: if it holds for L it holds for every larger L, so the feasible values form a suffix and binary search can find its left boundary. Testing one L is a linear greedy scan: accumulate elements into the current part, and whenever adding the next element would exceed L, close the part and start a new one; feasible if the resulting count is at most k. The greedy is optimal because closing a part later is never worse. Total cost is O(n log(sum - max)). The transferable idea is the shape - a monotone yes/no predicate over a numeric answer - which is what makes minimum-capacity, minimum-speed and minimum-time problems all the same problem.
follow_up_seeds: Why is the greedy feasibility check optimal for a fixed L?

text: Binary search is famously easy to get wrong. Describe the loop invariant your implementation maintains, explain how you decide between lo <= hi and lo < hi as the loop condition, and say why computing the midpoint as (lo + hi) / 2 is a latent bug in a fixed-width integer language.

expected_concepts.hint: the target, if present, always lies within the current search interval
the interval must shrink on every iteration or the loop hangs
lo + hi can exceed the integer range; use lo + (hi - lo) / 2
the condition must match whether the interval is closed or half-open

common_misconceptions: believes overflow is impossible because both indices are valid array positions
mixes a half-open interval with an inclusive loop condition and loops forever
reference_answer: State the invariant first and the rest follows: if the target is in the array, it is in the current interval. With a closed interval [lo, hi] the loop must run while lo <= hi, because a one-element interval lo == hi still needs to be examined, and the branches must move past the midpoint - lo = mid + 1 or hi = mid - 1 - so the interval strictly shrinks and the loop terminates. With a half-open interval [lo, hi) the condition is lo < hi and the update is hi = mid, which is correct only because mid < hi always holds under floor division. Mixing the two conventions is the classic infinite loop: hi = mid with lo <= hi never terminates when lo == hi. On the midpoint, lo + hi can exceed the maximum signed integer even though lo and hi are both valid indices - the famous bug in java.util.Arrays.binarySearch, live for nine years. Writing lo + (hi - lo) / 2 computes the same value without an intermediate that can overflow. Python's arbitrary-precision ints make this specific bug impossible, which is worth saying rather than pretending the concern is universal.
follow_up_seeds: How would you adapt it to find the first element greater than a target?

text: A stream of one billion numbers arrives and you must report the 100 largest, using memory proportional to 100 rather than to the length of the stream. Describe how a heap solves this, say whether you would use a min-heap or a max-heap and why that way round, and give the total time complexity.

expected_concepts.hint: maintain a bounded heap of the best k seen so far
a min-heap of size k, because the element to evict is the smallest kept
single pass, O(k) memory, cannot sort or store the input
O(n log k), against O(n log n) for sorting everything

common_misconceptions: reaches for a max-heap of size k, which makes the eviction candidate the wrong element
proposes sorting the stream, which violates the memory constraint
reference_answer: Keep a min-heap holding at most 100 elements. Push each incoming number; once the heap holds 101, pop the minimum. At any moment the heap contains the 100 largest elements seen so far, and at the end it is the answer. The counterintuitive part is that finding the largest elements uses a min-heap: the only element you ever need to look at is the weakest of the ones you are keeping, since that is the one a new arrival must beat, and a min-heap puts exactly that element at the root in O(1). A max-heap would expose the largest kept element, which is never the one under threat. Cost is O(log k) per element, O(n log k) overall with k = 100, and O(k) memory - independent of the one billion, which is what the memory constraint demands. A cheap and worthwhile optimisation is to compare against the root before pushing and skip the push entirely when the new value is smaller, which makes the common case O(1). Sorting the stream would be O(n log n) time and, fatally here, O(n) memory.
follow_up_seeds: How would you merge the results of running this on ten machines?

text: Given n intervals with start and end times, repeatedly choosing the interval with the earliest end time yields a maximum-size set of non-overlapping intervals. Explain why this greedy choice is provably optimal rather than merely plausible, and describe a scheduling variant in which the same greedy strategy stops being optimal.

expected_concepts.hint: some optimal solution contains the earliest-finishing interval
swap the first interval of any optimal solution for the greedy one without loss
sort by end time, take an interval whenever it starts after the last one taken
weighted intervals break it; that variant needs dynamic programming

common_misconceptions: justifies the greedy by trying examples rather than by an exchange argument
assumes sorting by start time or by shortest duration is equally valid
reference_answer: The proof is an exchange argument. Let g be the interval with the earliest end time and let O be any optimal solution, with o its first interval by end time. Since g ends no later than o, replacing o with g in O leaves every remaining interval in O still compatible - they all start after o ends, hence after g ends - so O' = O minus o plus g is also optimal and has the same size. Some optimal solution therefore contains the greedy choice, and applying the argument inductively to the remaining subproblem shows the greedy solution is optimal overall. This is what distinguishes a proof from examples: it quantifies over all optimal solutions rather than testing a few inputs. Choosing earliest end time is what leaves the maximum room for the rest, which is why sorting by start time or by shortest duration both fail - a single early-starting interval that runs all day, or a short interval overlapping two disjoint ones, defeats them. The greedy also fails as soon as intervals carry weights and the objective becomes maximum total weight: one high-value long interval can beat many cheap short ones, there is no exchange argument, and the correct solution is a dynamic program over intervals sorted by end time using a predecessor lookup.
follow_up_seeds: Sketch the DP recurrence for the weighted version.

text: For the 0/1 knapsack problem, a candidate proposes sorting items by value per unit weight and taking them greedily until the bag is full. Give a small instance where this produces a suboptimal answer, then state the dynamic-programming recurrence that solves the problem correctly, with its time and space complexity.

expected_concepts.hint: indivisible items make the ratio greedy leave unusable capacity
dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w], value[i] + dp[i-1][w - weight[i]])
the best packing of the first i items is built from the best packing of i-1
O(n * W) is polynomial in W's value but exponential in its bit length

common_misconceptions: assumes the fractional-knapsack greedy carries over to the 0/1 version
calls the O(n * W) table polynomial time without qualification
reference_answer: A counterexample: capacity 10, with item A of weight 6 and value 7 (ratio 1.17) and items B and C each of weight 5 and value 5 (ratio 1.0). The ratio greedy takes A, then cannot fit either of the others, and scores 7; taking B and C scores 10. The greedy is optimal for fractional knapsack, where the leftover capacity can be filled with a fraction of the next item, and that is precisely the step indivisibility removes. The correct solution is dp[i][w] = the best value using the first i items with capacity w, computed as max(dp[i-1][w], value[i] + dp[i-1][w - weight[i]]) when weight[i] <= w and dp[i-1][w] otherwise, with dp[0][w] = 0. It relies on optimal substructure - the optimum over i items decomposes into the optimum over i - 1 - and on overlapping subproblems, which is what makes tabulation pay. Cost is O(n * W) time and O(n * W) space, reducible to O(W) by keeping one row and iterating w downward so each item is used at most once. O(n * W) is pseudo-polynomial, not polynomial: W is a number, and its encoding is logarithmic in its value, which is why 0/1 knapsack is still NP-hard.
follow_up_seeds: Why must the one-dimensional version iterate the capacity downward?

text: Contrast top-down memoisation with bottom-up tabulation for the same dynamic-programming problem: what each computes, how they differ in which subproblems get evaluated at all, and when you would prefer one over the other. Then explain how a table indexed by two variables can often be reduced to memory proportional to one of them.

expected_concepts.hint: recursion with a cache versus an explicit iteration over the state space
memoisation touches only reachable states; tabulation fills all of them
if row i depends only on row i-1, keep two rows and reuse them
O(n * m) becomes O(m), at the cost of losing the traceback

common_misconceptions: believes the two approaches always evaluate the same set of subproblems
applies the rolling-array trick while still needing to reconstruct the solution path
reference_answer: Both compute the same recurrence. Memoisation writes it as recursion and caches each result on first computation, so only the subproblems actually reachable from the initial call are ever evaluated - a real saving when the state space is large but sparsely used. Tabulation iterates the state space in an order that guarantees dependencies are ready before they are needed, filling every cell whether or not it matters. Tabulation avoids recursion depth limits and call overhead and has better memory locality, which usually makes it faster in practice; memoisation is easier to write when the dependency order is awkward to express as loops, and is the natural choice when the reachable fraction of states is small. Neither changes the asymptotic time. For space: if dp[i][*] depends only on dp[i-1][*], the older rows are dead and you can keep two rows, or a single row updated in the correct direction, reducing O(n * m) to O(m). The cost is that the discarded rows are exactly what a traceback would need, so this works when only the optimal value is wanted; recovering the actual solution needs the full table, stored decisions, or a divide-and-conquer reconstruction such as Hirschberg's algorithm.

text: Distinguish worst-case, average-case and amortised complexity as three different kinds of claim. Give one data-structure operation whose amortised cost is far better than its worst-case cost, and explain why quoting the average case would be the wrong claim to make about it.

expected_concepts.hint: a worst-case guarantee over a sequence of operations, with no probability involved
an expectation over a distribution of inputs, which an adversary can violate
a bound on any single operation on any input
the three quantify over different things; using one to mean another misleads

common_misconceptions: treats amortised as a synonym for average or typical
believes an amortised bound implies anything about a single operation's latency
reference_answer: The three differ in what they quantify over. Worst case bounds a single operation over all inputs. Average case is an expectation over an assumed distribution of inputs, so it says nothing about an adversarially chosen input - which is why hash-table denial-of-service attacks work despite the O(1) average. Amortised bounds the total cost of a sequence of operations divided by their number, and it is a worst-case statement: no input sequence, adversarial or otherwise, exceeds it, and no probability is involved anywhere. Appending to a dynamic array is the standard example: an individual append that triggers a resize is O(n), yet any sequence of n appends costs O(n) in total, so append is O(1) amortised. Average case would be the wrong claim because it implies a distributional assumption the structure does not need - the guarantee is deterministic. The distinction has a practical consequence: an amortised bound says nothing about any individual operation's latency, so a system with a hard per-request deadline, or one measured on p99 rather than throughput, may be unable to accept a structure with an excellent amortised bound and an occasional O(n) pause.
